title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Identify the stepped link as an axial load-transfer member.
student: State the primary structural function of the stepped steel link in the industrial assembly.
instructor: The link transfers axial tensile force between structural brackets or machine-frame attachment points while maintaining the required alignment and load path.
gradingNotes: Students should identify a tensile load-transfer function rather than beam bending.

title: External Loads
learningObjectives: Identify the external loading that produces axial tension.
student: Identify where the external loads act and describe their directions.
instructor: Equal and opposite centered axial forces P act at the two ends. They place all three segments in axial tension.

title: Supports and Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Represent physical end connections in a two-force-member model.
student: How are the pinned or bolted end connections represented in the simplified model?
instructor: The brackets or pins are replaced by equal and opposite axial forces applied through the member axis. A separate support-reaction calculation is unnecessary for this isolated two-force member.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace force through changing cross-sectional areas.
student: Trace the tensile load through the link from one connection to the other.
instructor: The load enters one end segment, passes through its transition into center segment BC, crosses the second transition, and exits through the opposite end segment. The internal axial-force magnitude is the same in every segment, but average stress changes with area.

title: Expected Governing Section
student: Which constant-area section is expected to govern the allowable axial load, and why?
instructor: {{link_critical_section}} {{link_critical_verb}} the allowable load because the governing area is the minimum, {{link_critical_area_mm2}} mm2. Local fillet stress concentration is excluded from the base model.

title: Relevant Mechanical Responses
student: Identify and rank the mechanical responses considered in this problem.
instructor: Average axial normal stress compared with allowable stress controls maximum load. Total axial elongation is a secondary stiffness or serviceability response. Buckling is not relevant because the member is in tension.

title: Relevant Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify inputs required for allowable load and elongation.
student: Identify the geometric and material parameters required to determine maximum load and total elongation.
instructor: Required inputs are σallow, thickness t, widths w1 and w2, lengths LAB, LBC, and LCD, and modulus E. Radius r is displayed but does not enter the base calculation because local fillet effects are neglected.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Convert the industrial link into a three-segment axial model.
student: Before using the reference figure, draw a simplified Mechanics of Materials model showing three constant-area segments, uniform thickness, segment lengths, and equal and opposite axial loads.
instructor: A correct model shows narrow segment AB, center segment BC, end segment CD, uniform thickness t, and centered tensile loads P. Each segment carries the same internal axial force.
gradingNotes: The student model should preserve the axial load path without unnecessary bracket geometry.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions supporting a prismatic-segment model.
student: State the assumptions used to simplify the real component.
instructor: Assume centered axial load, linear-elastic material, small deformation, uniform average stress in each prismatic segment, constant thickness, negligible self-weight, and no connection or local fillet stress-concentration effects.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
learningObjectives: Plan the strength and deformation calculation sequence.
student: Describe the calculation sequence needed to determine maximum load and total elongation.
instructor: Calculate each segment area; identify the minimum area; determine Pmax = σallowAmin; calculate each segment elongation PL/(AE) at that load; then sum the three contributions and interpret the result.

title: Boundary Conditions and Internal Force
learningObjectives: Relate end loads to internal force in each segment.
student: From the instructor reference diagram, identify the boundary loading and internal axial force carried by each segment.
instructor: Equal and opposite loads P pull the link ends. A cut through AB, BC, or CD gives internal axial force N = P in tension.

title: Cross-Sectional Areas
learningObjectives: Calculate cross-sectional areas from width and thickness.
student: Calculate the cross-sectional area of each constant-width segment.
commonMistakes: Use the out-of-plane plate thickness t; radius r is not a thickness.

title: Critical Section for Strength
learningObjectives: Identify the section controlling allowable load.
student: Identify the critical constant-area section for the allowable-load calculation and justify your selection.
instructor: {{link_critical_section}} {{link_critical_verb}} because the governing area, {{link_critical_area_mm2}} mm2, is the minimum. Under the same internal force, the minimum-area section has the largest average normal stress.

title: Maximum Allowable Axial Load
learningObjectives: Calculate allowable load from allowable stress and governing area.
student: Using σallow = {{sigma_allow}} {{sigma_allow_unit}}, determine the maximum allowable axial tensile load.
instructor: Pmax = σallowAmin = {{link_pmax_N}} N = {{link_pmax_kN}} kN. At this load, stresses are {{link_stress_AB_MPa}} MPa in AB, {{link_stress_BC_MPa}} MPa in BC, and {{link_stress_CD_MPa}} MPa in CD.
gradingNotes: With MPa = N/mm2, multiplying stress by area directly gives force in newtons.

title: Elongation of Each Segment
learningObjectives: Calculate deformation of each prismatic segment.
student: At P = Pmax, calculate the elongation of segments AB, BC, and CD.

title: Total Link Elongation
learningObjectives: Sum axial deformations of serial member segments.
student: Calculate the total elongation of the stepped link at the maximum allowable load.
commonMistakes: All three serial-segment elongations contribute to the end-to-end displacement.

title: Stiffness Interpretation
learningObjectives: Explain why the strength-governing section may differ from the dominant deformation segment.
student: Which segment contributes most to total elongation, and why can that differ from the section governing strength?
instructor: Segment {{link_dominant_segment}} contributes the most, {{link_dominant_elongation_mm}} mm. Strength depends on minimum area through P/A, whereas elongation depends on each segment's L/A ratio. A longer segment can dominate deformation even when its area is larger.

title: Strength-Based Modification
learningObjectives: Recommend a modification that directly increases allowable load.
student: If a larger allowable tensile load is required, identify a direct geometry or material modification and justify it.
instructor: {{link_strength_modification}} A material with a higher allowable stress can also increase load capacity. Increasing only a non-governing area does not raise Pmax.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Summarize strength and deformation results with appropriate limitations.
student: Summarize the allowable-load and elongation results in a short engineering recommendation. State what remains outside the base model.
instructor: The link supports a maximum modeled tensile load of {{link_pmax_kN}} kN based on {{link_critical_section}}. Its predicted elongation at that load is {{link_delta_total_mm}} mm, with segment {{link_dominant_segment}} contributing most. This is suitable as a preliminary average-stress and deformation result. Final design requires fillet stress concentration, pin-hole net section, bearing, connection strength, fatigue, fracture, manufacturing tolerance, and applicable design-standard checks.
gradingNotes: The recommendation must not interpret the allowable-stress result as verification of omitted local or connection limit states.
